title: Uber Cuts 3,300 Jobs in Largest Layoffs Since COVID-Era Downturn
excerpt: The ride-hailing giant is slashing 10% of its workforce to flatten management layers and redirect investment toward robotaxis and autonomous vehicle technology.
body:
• Uber will lay off approximately 3,300 employees — 10% of its global workforce — in its largest reduction since the pandemic-era cuts of May 2020
  • CEO Dara Khosrowshahi is flattening management layers with a 20% reduction in managers, cutting micro-teams by half, and limiting remote roles to less than 1% of staff
  • The restructuring aims to redirect savings toward robotaxis, with Uber planning to invest more than $10 billion in autonomous vehicle technology in the coming years
  • Uber shares rose about 2% on the news, even as the stock has underperformed the S&P 500 this year with a nearly 8% decline

The Biggest Cuts Since COVID

Uber Technologies announced Wednesday that it will lay off about 3,300 employees, roughly 10% of its global workforce, in a sweeping restructuring designed to strip out management complexity and free up capital for its push into autonomous vehicles.

The layoffs, first reported by Bloomberg News, are Uber's largest since May 2020, when pandemic-driven demand collapse forced the company to shed 6,700 jobs — nearly a quarter of its staff. Uber had about 34,000 employees globally at the end of last year.

CEO Dara Khosrowshahi announced the changes in an email to employees, framing them as necessary despite strong business performance. Over the past five years, Uber's revenue has nearly tripled, but the growth has created layers of organizational complexity that now impede decision-making.

"A leaner organization will mean clearer ownership, faster decisions, and more time spent building rather than coordinating. It will also generate savings that we intend to reinvest in growth, innovation, and the capabilities that will matter most over the coming years."

— Dara Khosrowshahi, CEO, Uber Technologies

Flattening the Hierarchy

The restructuring targets Uber's managerial ranks specifically. The company will reduce the number of managers by 20%, with some transitioning to individual contributor roles. Teams with only one or two direct reports — so-called micro-teams — are being cut by nearly 50%. Employees positioned seven or more reporting layers below the CEO will see a 20% reduction.

Uber is also combining its engineering, science and delivery divisions, and consolidating delivery operations across restaurants, retail and direct divisions into a single unit. The company will concentrate staff in a smaller number of key hubs and limit fully remote roles to about 1% of employees, while maintaining its existing three-day office attendance policy.

Robotaxi Competition Looms Large

While Khosrowshahi did not cite AI as a reason for the cuts — unlike several other tech executives this year — the restructuring is widely seen as Uber's response to the growing threat from autonomous ride-hailing.

Waymo, the biggest U.S. robotaxi operator, currently runs its autonomous vehicles through Uber's app in Austin and Atlanta, but has been expanding into new markets independently. Tesla is also doubling down on robotaxis, feeding investor fears that a growing fleet of driverless cars could erode Uber's lucrative middleman position.

To counter the threat, Uber plans to invest more than $10 billion in robotaxis in the coming years, backing autonomous-driving developers and positioning itself as a marketplace for driverless rides. The company recently partnered with Hertz to build robotaxi fleets and inked a $1.25 billion deal with Rivian.

Pressure on Multiple Fronts

Beyond robotaxis, Uber faces mounting competition in food delivery. DoorDash, Instacart and local delivery platforms have been pressuring Uber Eats, prompting the company to acquire Delivery Hero for $14.8 billion to build scale.

The company is also grappling with runaway AI costs, having reportedly burned through its entire 2026 technology budget for AI in just four months. Uber's stock has underperformed both the S&P 500 and rival Lyft this year, declining nearly 8%.

Tracking website layoffs.fyi estimates that more than 123,000 tech workers have been laid off across nearly 390 companies in 2026 so far, as the industry continues to restructure around AI adoption and efficiency mandates.

Uber shares rose roughly 2% following the announcement on Wednesday. Rival Lyft advanced 3.3%.
